summary.text: An 18-year-old young adult with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, spastic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level V) after preterm birth at 26 weeks, contractures, scoliosis, hip dysplasia, epilepsy, hypothyroidism and underweight had resuscitation for severe sepsis at age 16. He had severe musculoskeletal pain from spasticity and hip luxation.

Oral morphine 2 mg four times a day was started via gastric tube alongside 13 other substances. Body weight was 33.2 kg and BMI 16.8 kg/m² (2nd percentile). The daily oral morphine equivalent dose was 0.241 mg/kg/d.

On day two of treatment he developed oxygen desaturation (lowest saturation 82%) and a reduced respiratory rate of 7/min requiring repeated stimulation, diagnosed as opioid-induced respiratory depression; morphine was discontinued. Two days after the incident he developed pneumonia, with antibiotic treatment necessitated.

A second opioid trial with oral levomethadone was titrated up to 0.5 mg twice daily under close pulse oximetry and respiratory rate monitoring until sufficient pain relief was achieved, without signs of respiratory depression.

summary.text: A 15-year-old adolescent with Ohtahara syndrome and spastic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level V), obstructive sleep apnea, contractures and type I respiratory failure was admitted to the PPC unit for severe neuroirritability with pain-like behavior and seizures. Weight was 23.5 kg, length 105 cm and BMI 21.3 kg/m².

Because of a possible central neuropathic pain component of therapy-refractory agitation, oral levomethadone 2.5 mg three times daily was started via gastric tube alongside a comedication of 10 substances. After one day it was paused for increased myoclonus, seizures and oxygen desaturations.

A second attempt with levomethadone 1 mg orally three times daily led, on day 8 of therapy, to increased apnea phases and oxygen desaturations requiring repeated stimulation and oxygen supply, consistent with opioid-induced respiratory depression. The oral morphine equivalent dose was 1.02 mg/kg/d; Table 3 gives a lowest oxygen saturation of 88% without stating which episode.
Further into the inpatient course a slower levomethadone titration up to 3.25 mg orally three times a day achieved a decrease in the frequency and extent of painful agitation.

summary.text: A 20-year-old young adult with lissencephaly, spastic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level V), a cognitive developmental age of less than 12 months, severe underweight (BMI 13.8 kg/m²), severe obstructive sleep apnea and a ventriculoatrial shunt had severe musculoskeletal pain secondary to spasticity and hip dysplasia, refractory to oral tilidine with naloxone. He had no gastric tube.

A transdermal buprenorphine 5 µg/h patch was started as a long-acting alternative while he was concomitantly treated with 12 different substances. On the night of the first day he had repeated oxygen desaturations (lowest saturation 58%) requiring repeated stimulation, oxygen supply and patch removal, consistent with opioid-induced respiratory depression.

Over the remainder of the inpatient course the dose was carefully titrated by cutting the matrix patch into quarters. An increase to a 5 µg/h patch was initiated but reduced to 3.75 µg/h because of repeated fatigue.
